title: Why Manners?
summary: Hosts discuss manners and etiquette: how they differ, how they are culturally bound, and why they are often described as the glue holding civilization together. Topics include the Egyptian vizier Ptahhotep's advice, the Cynic philosopher Diogenes' rejection of manners, Erasmus's 1530 guide on civility for children, the origin of the word etiquette in French courts, Lord Chesterfield's letters to his son, Emily Post's 1922 etiquette book and her role in exposing a blackmail ring, Miss Manners, the politics of respectability, cross-cultural differences in punctuality, eye contact, food offering and personal space, the decline of traditional table manners, smoking etiquette, and modern texting and dating etiquette. The episode ends with a listener mail response about King Leopold II and the Congo Free State.
topics: Etiquette in Society in Business and at Home

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Hosts open the episode and tease the topic of manners.

segments.title: Defining manners and etiquette
segments.summary: Manners are culturally bound expectations of polite behavior, often ingrained from childhood; etiquette is more formal, learned from books or instruction. Ptahhotep's retirement letter of life and manners advice is introduced.

segments.title: Manners as the glue of civilization and Diogenes
segments.summary: Manners are described as unwritten rules holding society together, including prohibitions on violence and small courtesies. Diogenes the Cynic rejected manners as hypocritical masks and engaged in shocking public behavior to make his point.

segments.title: Cultural variation and food hospitality
segments.summary: Manners are culturally bound; the Ju/'hoansi hunters are criticized for bringing back meat to keep them humble. Native American hospitality with a perpetual stew pot is contrasted with European formal meal times.

segments.title: Offering food repeatedly
segments.summary: Hosts discuss cultures where guests decline food several times before accepting, with examples from the American South and Italian families in the Northeast.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Renaissance manners and Erasmus
segments.summary: Manners changed over time, with shame developing from the medieval era through the nineteenth century, per Norbert Elias. Erasmus wrote a 1530 civility guide advising against stirring gravy with fingers, blowing noses on tablecloths, and wiping spoons used for communal soup. A joke about covering a fart with a cough follows.

segments.title: Etiquette origins and royal courts
segments.summary: The word etiquette is traced to French courts, with theories about tickets, labels, and signs at Versailles. Marie Antoinette reportedly nicknamed a retainer Madame Etiquette. Court instructions were printed, and the word entered English in the mid-1700s.

segments.title: Lord Chesterfield's letters to his son
segments.summary: Philip Dormer Stanhope, fourth Earl of Chesterfield, wrote letters to his illegitimate son with manners advice, praised as witty and insightful but also criticized as cynical. The hosts discuss social climbing and the democratizing potential of learning etiquette, with movie examples.

segments.title: Emily Post and American etiquette
segments.summary: American etiquette developed in the Gilded Age, and Emily Post's 1922 book became highly successful. Her three principles were consideration, respect, and honesty. The hosts describe how she exposed a New York blackmail ring targeting her husband's affair, at personal cost.

segments.title: Miss Manners and the politics of respectability
segments.summary: Judith Martin's Miss Manners column began in 1978. Historian Evelyn Brooks Higginbotham's term politics of respectability is discussed in relation to Black women in the progressive era and Civil Rights protests.

segments.title: Ad break
segments.summary: Second ad break.

segments.title: Universal manners and cross-cultural communication
segments.summary: Hierarchy of superiors, equals and inferiors is described as a near-universal concept. Edward T. Hall's 1955 observations on how Americans are perceived abroad, including voice volume and formal introductions, are discussed.

segments.title: Punctuality across cultures
segments.summary: Punctuality norms vary, with Australia and New Zealand strict and Indian weddings more relaxed. A personal anecdote about padding arrival times for punctual-challenged friends.

segments.title: Eye contact norms
segments.summary: Appropriate eye contact in the United States is contrasted with the UK, where less eye contact is considered normal. Hosts share how overthinking eye contact backfires.

segments.title: Shaquille O'Neal photo shoot anecdote
segments.summary: Chuck recounts a photo shoot in which Shaquille O'Neal arrived hours early and then wanted to leave early to pick up his daughter, which shifted the schedule. Josh jokes about the shoot timing.

segments.title: Foreign views of American manners and traditional manners declining
segments.summary: A travel article describing American manners is discussed. The hosts argue traditional table rules like fork use and keeping elbows off the table are outdated, while manners and etiquette have evolved.

segments.title: Smoking etiquette
segments.summary: Smoking is considered rude in many settings; about eleven percent of Americans smoke. The hosts recall smoking on airplanes and cite countries with the highest smoking rates, including Nauru and Kiribati.

segments.title: Texting, ghosting and dating etiquette
segments.summary: A list of modern etiquette rules is discussed, including a 72-hour grace period for explaining slow text replies, ghosting norms, tipping, and bar behavior. Poor manners are described as a red flag in dating, and Emily Post's principles are revisited.

segments.title: Listener mail: King Leopold II and the Congo Free State
segments.summary: A listener named John adds detail to the International Debt Forgiveness episode, citing the Sebastian Major Fake History episodes on Leopold II's propaganda and the Free State of Congo. Hosts mention Behind the Bastards.

segments.summary: Closing credits and listener contact information.
